scenes.head: Debt schedules
scenes.sub: Every loan has its own timetable of interest and repayments, and a line of credit fills whatever gap is left. Build Lantern’s debt schedule loan by loan, let the line of credit balance the cash, keep the model free of circular references, and measure whether the business can carry its debt.

segs.say: Debt schedules. Every loan has its own timetable of interest and repayments, and a line of credit fills whatever gap is left. Build Lantern’s debt schedule loan by loan, let the line of credit balance the cash, keep the model free of circular references, and measure whether the business can carry its debt.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Build a debt schedule for each loan: opening balance, drawings, repayments, closing balance and interest for each year.
Calculate the interest and principal of an amortising loan for part of a year from its payment schedule.
Use a line of credit as a revolver that keeps cash at a minimum balance within a limit, and explain the funding gap when the limit is reached.
Explain how charging interest on opening balances avoids circular references, and what it costs in accuracy.
Calculate the current portion of long-term debt and the debt service coverage ratio, and interpret them for a lender.

scenes.head: At the end of 2027 Lantern owes money four ways: the first Coastline note ($10,000, due on 1 March 2028), the van note ($15,000, repaid $5,000 each…

segs.say: At the end of 2027 Lantern owes money four ways: the first Coastline note ($10,000, due on 1 March 2028), the van note ($15,000, repaid $5,000 each June), the cold-brew brewer’s instalment plan ($16,250), and $24,000 drawn on Coastline’s $30,000 line of credit. In March 2028 it adds a fifth: the $60,000 term loan for the second kitchen, repaid monthly over five years. Hollis Avery also pays $75,000 for 30% of the company. Coastline wants to see each of these in the model, with every payment on the right date.

scenes.head: A debt schedule sets out, for each loan and each year, the balance at the start, any new borrowing, the repayments, the balance at the end and the…

segs.say: A debt schedule sets out, for each loan and each year, the balance at the start, any new borrowing, the repayments, the balance at the end and the interest. Loans with different terms need their own rows, because they are repaid on different timetables at different rates, and because the covenant and the balance sheet need to know how much of each is due within a year. The total of all the schedules gives the model’s interest expense, its debt repayments in the cash flow statement and its debt on the balance sheet.

scenes.head: Lantern’s loans show the three common shapes.

segs.say: Lantern’s loans show the three common shapes. The first Coastline note is a bullet: interest only, then the whole $10,000 at maturity. The van note repays a fixed $5,000 of principal each year with interest on the balance. The brewer plan and the new term loan are amortising loans: level payments that each cover the month’s interest and repay some principal, a little more each month.

chapters.title: The term loan, month by month into years

scenes.head: Coastline lends $60,000 on 31 March 2028 at 7.5% a year, repaid in 60 equal monthly payments at each month end from 30 April.

segs.say: Coastline lends $60,000 on 31 March 2028 at 7.5% a year, repaid in 60 equal monthly payments at each month end from 30 April. The payment comes from the annuity formula of F04: 60,000 × 0.00625 ÷ (1 − 1.00625⁻⁶⁰) = 1,202.28 dollars. The first payment carries 0.625% of $60,000, $375.00, of interest and repays $827.28. An annual model needs the totals for each calendar year, so it adds up the months: 2028 has nine payments (April to December), with interest of $3,186.12 and principal of $7,634.37, leaving $52,365.63 owed at the end of the year.

scenes.head: This is the reliable way to put any loan into an annual model: build its schedule at the frequency it is actually paid (monthly here), then sum each…

segs.say: This is the reliable way to put any loan into an annual model: build its schedule at the frequency it is actually paid (monthly here), then sum each calendar year’s interest and principal, and read off the balance at each year end. Approximating with an annual rate on an annual balance would get the first year badly wrong, because the loan exists for only nine months of it.

chapters.title: The line of credit as the balancing item

scenes.head: A model forecasts every flow of cash except one: how much the business must borrow at short notice, or can repay, to end each year with the cash it…

segs.say: A model forecasts every flow of cash except one: how much the business must borrow at short notice, or can repay, to end each year with the cash it needs. That job goes to a revolver, a revolving line of credit the model draws on and repays automatically. Ana sets a minimum cash balance of $15,000, enough for a month of wages and suppliers. Each year the model works out the cash Lantern would have before the line moves; if that is below the minimum, it draws the difference, and if above, it repays the line, never below zero and never above the $30,000 limit.
Line of creditₜ = min (Limit, max (0, Lineₜ₋₁ + Minimum cash − Cash before the lineₜ))

scenes.head: In 2028 Lantern’s cash before the line moves would be $33,259: the $6,531 it starts with, plus cash from operations, less the kitchen spending and…

segs.say: In 2028 Lantern’s cash before the line moves would be $33,259: the $6,531 it starts with, plus cash from operations, less the kitchen spending and repayments, plus the term loan and Hollis’s money. That is more than the $15,000 minimum, so $18,259 can go to the line, cutting it from $24,000 to $5,741. In 2029 the remaining $5,741 is repaid in full.

chapters.title: Reading the term sheet into the model

scenes.head: A new loan’s terms come from the lender’s term sheet, and each term has a place in the schedule.

segs.say: A new loan’s terms come from the lender’s term sheet, and each term has a place in the schedule. The amount and the date it is drawn give the drawing and the first year’s months. The rate, and whether it is fixed or floating, gives the interest; a floating rate needs its own input row for each year, so that a rise in rates can be tested. The repayment profile (amortising, fixed principal, or a bullet at maturity) gives the principal each year. Fees paid to arrange the loan are a cost on the day it is drawn. And the covenants, such as Coastline’s current ratio of at least 1.2, become output rows that the model tests every period. Coastline’s term sheet for Lantern is simple: a fixed rate, level monthly payments and one covenant.

chapters.title: Interest owed at the year end

scenes.head: Interest expense and interest paid are not always the same in a year.

segs.say: Interest expense and interest paid are not always the same in a year. Lantern’s van note pays its interest once a year, each 1 June, so at 31 December seven months of interest have been charged but not paid: $350 at the end of 2028, a current liability called interest payable. The brewer plan pays each month’s interest at the start of the next month, so one month is owed at each year end. The term loan and the line of credit pay within the month, so nothing is owed. The model works out the interest owed at each year end loan by loan; the cash paid in the year is then the expense plus what was owed at the start, less what is owed at the end. Lantern owed $819 at the end of 2027, all of it paid early in 2028.

scenes.head: Lantern’s debt schedule for 2028

segs.say: Each loan in 2028 (dollars)

scenes.head: Interest for 2028 totals $6,632: $4,472 on the four fixed loans and $2,160 on the line of credit.

segs.say: Interest for 2028 totals $6,632: $4,472 on the four fixed loans and $2,160 on the line of credit. Each loan is charged for the months it is outstanding: the first note for January and February only ($100), the van note on $15,000 for five months and on $10,000 for seven ($725).

chapters.title: Circular references, and how the model avoids them

scenes.head: The line of credit creates a loop if the model is careless.

segs.say: The line of credit creates a loop if the model is careless. Its interest depends on its balance; the balance depends on how much cash the business needs; the cash need depends on profit; and profit depends on interest. If interest were charged on the average of the opening and closing balances, the formulas would refer to each other in a circle. Excel can solve such a loop by iteration, but circular models are slow, can fail to settle, and make every error harder to trace.

scenes.head: Lantern’s model breaks the loop by charging the line’s interest on its opening balance: 9% × $24,000 = $2,160 for 2028.

segs.say: Lantern’s model breaks the loop by charging the line’s interest on its opening balance: 9% × $24,000 = $2,160 for 2028. The opening balance is already known when the year starts, so nothing loops. The cost is accuracy: Lantern repays most of the line during 2028, so interest on the average balance would be lower. For a small line the difference is small, and the model says which convention it uses. Larger models often compute interest on the average balance and break the circle with a switch that turns the calculation off, or with a copy-and-paste routine, but the principle is the same: never leave a circular reference without a reason and a way to break it.

chapters.title: What is due within a year

scenes.head: The balance sheet splits each loan into the current portion of long-term debt, the principal due in the next twelve months, and the rest.

segs.say: The balance sheet splits each loan into the current portion of long-term debt, the principal due in the next twelve months, and the rest. The debt schedule supplies it directly: the current portion at 31 December 2028 is next year’s principal. For Lantern it is $5,000 of the van note, $4,159 of the brewer plan (its last payments) and $10,868 of the term loan, together $20,027. That figure matters more than its size suggests, because Coastline’s covenant divides current assets by current liabilities, and the current portion is a current liability. Repaying debt faster can therefore make the current ratio worse before it makes it better.

chapters.title: Can the business carry its debt?

scenes.head: Lenders look at two kinds of measure.

segs.say: Lenders look at two kinds of measure. Leverage measures compare the debt with the business’s earnings or value: debt to EBITDA, or debt to equity. Coverage measures compare what the business earns with what its debt costs each year. The most common for a term loan is the debt service coverage ratio, earnings available to pay debt divided by the interest and scheduled principal due. Definitions vary from lender to lender; a simple one uses EBITDA.
DSCRₜ = EBITDAₜ/(Interestₜ + Scheduled principalₜ)

scenes.head: Lantern’s DSCR is 0.56 in 2028 and 3.45 in 2029, rising to 10.64 by 2032.

segs.say: Lantern’s DSCR is 0.56 in 2028 and 3.45 in 2029, rising to 10.64 by 2032. The 2028 figure is below 1: EBITDA does not cover that year’s interest and repayments, which include repaying the whole first Coastline note and most of the brewer plan. The money comes from the new loan and Hollis’s equity, which is exactly what they were raised for, but a credit committee will want that said plainly. From 2029 the business covers its debt service more than three times over.

scenes.head: Equity is not in the debt schedule, but it is in the cash

segs.say: Equity is not in the debt schedule, but it is in the cash. Hollis Avery’s $75,000 for new shares is financing too. It goes to common stock on the balance sheet and to financing cash flows, not to the debt schedule, and it carries no interest or repayments. It is why Lantern can repay most of the line of credit in its loss year.

scenes.head: A loan’s balance, year by year

segs.say: A loan’s balance, year by year: Closingₜ = Openingₜ + Drawnₜ − Repaidₜ.
Drawnₜ: New borrowing in year t ($).
Repaidₜ: Principal repaid in year t (not interest) ($).
It assumes this: Interest is paid as it falls due, so it does not add to the balance.

scenes.head: Level payment on an amortising loan

segs.say: Level payment on an amortising loan: PMT = (P r)/(1−(1+r)⁻ⁿ).
P: The amount borrowed ($).
r: The interest rate per payment period (7.5% ÷ 12).
n: The number of payments.
It assumes this: Payments at the end of each period; the rate is fixed.
F04’s annuity formula, solved for the payment. In Excel: =PMT(7.5%/12,60,-60000).

scenes.head: The revolver

segs.say: The revolver: Lineₜ = min (Limit, max (0, Lineₜ₋₁ + Cₘᵢₙ − Cₜ^(before))).
Cₘᵢₙ: The minimum cash balance the business wants ($).
Cₜ^(before): Cash at the end of year t before the line is drawn or repaid ($).
Limit: The most the line allows ($).
It assumes this: If the formula would need more than the limit, the model shows a funding gap instead of inventing cash.

scenes.head: Debt service coverage ratio (a simple form)

segs.say: Debt service coverage ratio (a simple form): DSCR = EBITDA/(Interest + Scheduled principal).
Scheduled principal: Principal repayments due in the year under the loans’ terms ($).
It assumes this: Lenders define it differently (after tax, after maintenance capital spending); use the loan agreement’s definition when there is one.

scenes.head: The term loan’s first year

segs.say: Coastline lends $60,000 on 31 March 2028 at 7.5% a year, with 60 equal monthly payments from 30 April. Find the payment, the split of the first payment, and the balance at the end of 2028.

scenes.head: The term loan’s first year

segs.say: Step 2. First payment: interest 60,000 × 0.00625 = 375.00; principal 1,202.28 − 375.00 = 827.28.
Step 3. Nine payments fall in 2028. Summing the schedule: interest 3,186.12, principal 7,634.37; together 9 × 1,202.28 = 10,820.49.

scenes.head: The term loan’s first year

segs.say: Payment $1,202.28 a month; in 2028, interest $3,186.12 and principal $7,634.37; $52,365.63 owed at the year end.
Interest is front-loaded: in 2028 more than a quarter of what Lantern pays is interest; by 2032 almost all of it is principal.

chapters.title: Example: The line of credit in 2028 and 2029

scenes.head: The line of credit in 2028 and 2029

segs.say: Lantern starts 2028 with $24,000 drawn on its $30,000 line and wants at least $15,000 of cash at each year end. Before the line moves, the model shows cash of $33,259 at the end of 2028 and, with the 2028 line balance carried forward, $39,232 at the end of 2029. Find the line’s balance and interest each year.

scenes.head: The line of credit in 2028 and 2029

segs.say: Step 1. 2028: the formula gives max(0, 24,000 + 15,000 − 33,259) = 5,741, within the limit. Lantern repays 18,259 and ends with exactly 15,000 of cash.
Step 2. 2028 interest, on the opening balance: 24,000 × 9% = 2,160.
Step 3. 2029: max(0, 5,741 + 15,000 − 39,232) = max(0, -18,490) = 0. The line is repaid in full and cash ends at 33,490, above the minimum.
Step 4. 2029 interest, on the opening balance: 5,741 × 9% = 517.

scenes.head: The line of credit in 2028 and 2029

segs.say: $5,741 owed at the end of 2028 and nothing at the end of 2029; interest $2,160 and $517.
The line absorbs the timing of everything else. If the formula had asked for more than $30,000, Lantern would face a funding gap, a problem the model must show rather than hide.

scenes.head: What a credit committee sees

segs.say: Coastline’s credit committee looks at Lantern’s debt service each year. EBITDA is $23,319 in 2028 and $84,693 in 2029. Interest is $6,632 and $4,525; scheduled principal is $34,725 and $20,027. Calculate the DSCR and say what the committee should conclude.

scenes.head: What a credit committee sees

segs.say: Step 3. Explain 2028: its principal includes the $10,000 first note and $12,091 of the brewer plan, repaid from the new financing, not from EBITDA; operations alone do not cover it in the launch year.
Step 4. Look ahead: from 2029, coverage is 3.4 times and rising, which most lenders would regard as comfortable.

scenes.head: What a credit committee sees

segs.say: The committee will accept a weak first year if the model shows where the money comes from and the later years are strong. It will look next at the covenant, which depends on the balance sheet: lesson 6.

scenes.head: An amortising term loan in its first calendar year

segs.say: Coastline’s term loan as a Formula Explorer. Change the amount, rate, term and the month the first payment falls in, and watch the first year’s interest and principal and the year-end balance. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: Annual interest on an annual balance for a part year

segs.say: Annual interest on an annual balance for a part year. A loan drawn in March is outstanding for nine months of that year. Build the schedule at its payment frequency and sum the calendar year, or at least pro-rate by months.

scenes.head: Counting interest as repayment

segs.say: Counting interest as repayment. A loan payment is part interest (an expense) and part principal (a reduction in debt). Only the principal reduces the balance and goes to financing cash flows; the interest goes to the income statement.

scenes.head: A revolver with no limit

segs.say: A revolver with no limit. A line of credit that draws whatever the model needs hides a funding gap. Cap it at the agreed limit and show any shortfall in its own row.

scenes.head: Leaving a circular reference in place

segs.say: Leaving a circular reference in place. Interest on average balances makes the model loop. Charge interest on opening balances, or add a switch that breaks the circle, and say which you did.

scenes.head: Forgetting the current portion

segs.say: Forgetting the current portion. The principal due within a year is a current liability. Leaving it in long-term debt flatters the current ratio, which is exactly what a covenant tests.

scenes.head: Treating equity as debt

segs.say: Treating equity as debt. New shares bring cash but no interest or repayments. They belong in equity and financing cash flows, not in the debt schedule.

scenes.head: Banks build their own version of a borrower’s debt schedule before lending.

segs.say: Banks build their own version of a borrower’s debt schedule before lending. A credit analyst takes the term sheet, the existing loans from the accounts’ notes and the borrower’s forecast, and checks three things: that every existing loan is in the model with its real terms, that the new loan’s payments are right, and that the forecast does not quietly assume the line of credit is bigger than it is. Coverage and leverage ratios from the schedule then go into the bank’s internal rating, which sets the price of the loan.

scenes.head: In leveraged buyouts and project finance the debt schedule is the centre of the model: several layers of debt, cash sweeps that use spare cash to…

segs.say: In leveraged buyouts and project finance the debt schedule is the centre of the model: several layers of debt, cash sweeps that use spare cash to repay the most expensive layer first, and covenants tested every quarter. The principles are the ones in this lesson, applied to more loans.

scenes.head: Ana’s debt schedule shows Lantern’s debt falling from $72,266 at the end of 2028 to $3,562 by 2032, the line of credit repaid in 2029, and coverage…

segs.say: Ana’s debt schedule shows Lantern’s debt falling from $72,266 at the end of 2028 to $3,562 by 2032, the line of credit repaid in 2029, and coverage comfortable from 2029. What it cannot show on its own is whether the current ratio stays at 1.2. That needs the balance sheet, which the next lesson builds by linking the statements.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: A debt schedule gives each loan its own rows: opening balance, drawings, repayments, closing balance and interest for each year.
Build a loan at the frequency it is paid and sum each calendar year; part years matter.
An amortising loan’s level payment is P r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)−n); interest is front-loaded.
A revolver balances the model: it draws to keep cash at a minimum and repays when cash allows, within its limit; a need beyond the limit is a funding gap to show, not hide.
Charging interest on opening balances avoids circular references at a small cost in accuracy; state the convention.
The current portion of long-term debt is next year’s principal, a current liability that covenants count.
The debt service coverage ratio compares earnings with interest plus scheduled principal; read it with the reasons behind each year.
